chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, who said:

Ja'far ibn Muhammad wrote to him, asking him about travel and in what amount qasr prayer becomes due. So he wrote in his own handwriting—and I recognize it: Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام, when he travelled and went out on a journey, would shorten in one farsakh. Then the following year he repeated the question to him, so he wrote back to him: in ten days.

Thus, the sound way of understanding these two reports, including his statement, "he shortened in one farsakh," and other reports of the same kind, is that when the distance reaches the limit at which qasr becomes obligatory or more, then if the traveler travels for a day or more, or a farsakh, or less than that, or more, qasr becomes obligatory upon him, because the total distance has reached the limit in which qasr is obligatory. The consideration is not the amount a person travels at one time; rather, the consideration is the intended distance, even if he does not travel it in a single stretch. So this interpretation is not contradicted.

key_terms.السَّفَرِ: travel or journey that triggers legal rulings related to prayer
key_terms.الِاعْتِبَارُ: the operative legal consideration or criterion
key_terms.الْحَدِّ: the legal threshold at which qasr becomes obligatory
key_terms.الْمَسَافَةَ: the total travel distance considered in the ruling
key_terms.الْمَقْصُودَةِ: the intended destination-distance in view of the ruling
key_terms.الْمُسَافِرُ: the traveler subject to the ruling
key_terms.فَرْسَخٍ: a farsakh, a classical unit of travel distance

ai.seo_question: When does qasr prayer become obligatory for a traveler in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This report discusses the fiqh of travel and the threshold for performing qasr prayer. It explains that the legal criterion is the intended travel distance that reaches the prescribed limit, not necessarily how much of that distance is covered in a single stage or day.
